results.title:
Understanding cognitive impairment in multiple sclerosis using
                    structural and functional network measures and classification
                    algorithms
results.summary:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
<jats:p>Cognitive impairment (CI) is common in multiple sclerosis (MS), yet the network-level mechanisms underlying CI remain poorly understood. This study aimed to clarify how the joint organization of structural and functional brain networks contributes to CI in MS, and how network-derived features change when clinical information and MRI-derived measures are added. We analyzed neuropsychological and multimodal MRI data from the Amsterdam MS cohort (N = 330) and assessed generalizability externally (N = 27). Graph-theoretical measures of brain connectivity were extracted from diffusion-weighted and resting-state functional MRI. Machine learning models classified cognitively impaired versus preserved patients. Classification performance was quantified using the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROC), sensitivity, and specificity. Feature importance was evaluated using Shapley values. Network-derived features improved discrimination over demographic information alone (AUROC = 0.77; p < 0.001). Adding MRI-derived measures significantly improved performance (AUROC = 0.81; p < 0.001), whereas clinical variables added little additional information (AUROC = 0.79; p = 0.65). External validation demonstrated good discriminative ability (AUROC = 0.76) but low sensitivity. Structural connectivity within the dorsal attention network emerged as an informative feature. These findings suggest that network-derived features help classify cognitive status in MS and remain relevant alongside conventional features. Structural connectivity, especially within the dorsal attention network, may provide insight into systems-level correlates of CI in MS.</jats:p>

results.title: Explainable Deep Learning-Based Computer-Aided Differential Diagnosis of Multiple Sclerosis and Neuromyelitis Optica Using 3D MRI Lesion Features.
results.summary: Neurological disorders are among the leading causes of disability and mortality worldwide, making timely and accurate diagnosis essential. Differential diagnosis (DD) of Multiple Sclerosis (MS) and Neuromyelitis Optica (NMO) spectrum disorder using brain MRI remains challenging due to overlapping clinical manifestations and similar lesion characteristics. To address this challenge, this study proposes a neuroinformatics-driven computer-aided differential diagnosis (CADD) framework that automatically extracts, encodes, and analyzes quantitative 3D lesion biomarkers from brain MRI using deep learning and interpretable neuroimaging analytics. The proposed framework integrates three artificial intelligence (AI) modules: the NeuroImaging Sequence Examiner (NISE) for MRI sequence identification, the NeuroImaging Volumetric Extractor (NIVE) for skull stripping, and the NeuroImaging Lesion Extractor (NILE) for lesion segmentation. These modules are combined into an end-to-end neuroinformatics framework termed NeuroImaging Differential Evaluation (NIDE), which performs automated neuroimaging processing, lesion biomarker extraction, structured feature encoding, and differential diagnosis. Following lesion segmentation, quantitative 3D morphological and geometric lesion properties are extracted and transformed into a structured neuroimaging representation, where each row corresponds to an individual lesion and each column encodes a specific lesion biomarker. The resulting feature matrix is subsequently classified using a 2D convolutional neural network (2D-CNN). Comparative experiments against 3D-CNN models trained on raw MRI volumes, skull-stripped MRI volumes, lesion-mask volumes, and conventional machine learning classifiers demonstrate the superiority of the proposed lesion-driven learning strategy. Using ResNet50, the proposed framework achieved an accuracy of 80% for MS-NMO spectrum disorder differential diagnosis. Furthermore, the framework is independent of MRI view-plane orientation, enabling robust performance across different imaging orientations while operating in a fully automated manner. Beyond classification performance, the framework provides a structured representation of quantitative lesion biomarkers and enables interpretable neuroimaging analytics through Explainable Artificial Intelligence (XAI), with model interpretations corroborated by expert radiological assessment. The proposed NIDE framework demonstrates how automated neuroimaging processing, quantitative lesion characterization, structured feature encoding, and explainable AI can be integrated into a unified neuroinformatics workflow for differential diagnosis. These findings highlight the potential of neuroinformatics-driven decision-support systems for advancing neuroimaging analysis and clinical management of demyelinating neurological disorders.

results.title: Image-Level Classification of Central Vein Categories on FLAIR MRI in Multiple Sclerosis Using a Lightweight Explainable Deep Learning Framework.
results.summary: Background/Objectives: The central vein sign can help characterize multiple sclerosis (MS) lesions on MRI, but reading it takes specialist time and experience. We developed a compact convolutional neural network (CNN) and a deep feature engineering (DFE) pipeline for three-class classification of clinically labeled MR images. Methods: The MS Vein dataset contains 3181 axial FLAIR images from 154 participants in vein-positive, vein-negative, and control classes. MACDIBNeXt (about 6.5 million parameters) combines pooling-based attention downsampling, grouped convolution, and bottleneck and inverted bottleneck blocks. It was pretrained on Stable ImageNet1k and fine-tuned on a participant-level split (98 training, 25 validation, and 31 test participants). The DFE pipeline extracted 768 global average pooling features, selected 47 with CWINCA in participant-grouped folds of the training data, and classified them with tkNN. Results: On 635 held-out test images from 31 participants, the standalone CNN classified 527 correctly (82.99%; participant-cluster bootstrap 95% CI, 77.93-87.66%). DFE classified 571 correctly (89.92%; 85.47-93.82%), with 89.13% macro F1 and Cohen's κ of 0.83. With participants resampled as clusters, the 6.93-point gain had a 95% CI of 3.33-10.63 points (p = 0.0002), and a cluster-adjusted McNemar test gave p = 0.0021. Grad-CAM activation was intracranial in the displayed examples. Conclusions: MACDIBNeXt with DFE gives promising internal, image-level results. Because the data are retrospective, single-center, and labeled on FLAIR images, external participant-level validation is required before clinical use.

results.title: Novel Diagnostics for Cancer and Cognition: An Eye on "Smart" Mechanistic Pathways of Proliferation and Regulation.
results.summary: The global population is aging to the extent that over 450 million individuals will be greater than 80 years of age by the year 2050. As a result, an increase in non-communicable diseases that involve cancer and cognition is impacting individuals throughout the world and presents significant clinical challenges for health care professionals. Early detection and the ability to monitor disease outcomes are critical for cancer and cognitive loss and warrant the need for novel "smart" diagnostics that go beyond the assessment of total disease burden. Such diagnostics can monitor mechanistic proliferative and regulatory cellular pathways that offer additional avenues to develop innovative treatment strategies in conjunction with their diagnostic value. Cellular pathways that involve Wnt signaling, Wnt1 inducible signaling pathway protein 1 (WISP1), sirtuins, and non-coding ribonucleic acids (RNAs) provide exciting opportunities for the development of innovative diagnostics founded on underlying disease mechanisms for cancer and dementia. These diagnostic pathways hold intricate relationships with one another that alter biological and clinical outcomes, can be differentially expressed, and may require panel assessment with artificial intelligence and machine learning platforms. Future work will require evaluation in clinical subpopulations with specific comorbidities that necessitate in-depth validation and standardization for clinical translation.

results.title: AI-Assisted Follow-Up MRI Interpretation in Multiple Sclerosis: Radiology Residents' Diagnostic Confidence and Performance.
results.summary: Background/Objectives: Artificial intelligence (AI) tools are becoming increasingly utilised in everyday radiological practice. Evaluating follow-up magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of patients with multiple sclerosis (MS) is challenging. The aim of this study was to assess changes in confidence among four participating radiology residents when evaluating follow-up MRIs of MS patients using Pixyl.Neuro.MS® software. Methods: This retrospective study included 78 MS patients. Previous and new FLAIR images were independently analysed by four residents, first without AI and then in an immediate AI-assisted second reading using Pixyl.Neuro.MS®, a deep-learning lesion-segmentation software. Readers recorded their findings and confidence after each reading and rated the impact and usefulness of AI. The reference standard was defined by a consensus reading of a neuroradiologist and a radiology resident (15 and 4 years of experience). Paired analyses and patient-level bootstrap confidence intervals were used; bootstrap inference was conditional on the four readers. Results: The reference standard identified 24 patients with new lesions. Mean accuracy across readers increased from 84.62% to 90.71% (difference, 6.09 percentage points; 95% bootstrap confidence interval [CI], 2.24-10.26). Only Reader 3 showed a significant accuracy increase after Holm adjustment (p = 0.025). No accuracy comparison with routine reports was significant after adjustment. Confidence increased for all readers (all Holm-adjusted p < 0.001). Perceived usefulness did not differ significantly between lesion-burden groups. All readers predominantly rated the impact of AI as positive. The second-reading phase was shorter by a mean of 59.35 s (95% bootstrap CI, 51.39-67.07). Conclusions: In these four residents, the AI-assisted second reading was associated with higher confidence and average accuracy. The immediate sequential design prevents separation of AI contributions from familiarity and order effects, and the shorter second-reading phase does not establish an overall workflow time saving.

results.title: CNN-ViT-Based Model Incorporating a Voting-Based Ensemble Method with Future Fusion for Multiple Sclerosis Classification.
results.summary: Background/Objectives: Multiple Sclerosis (MS) is a chronic neurodegenerative disease affecting the central nervous system and significantly reducing the quality of life. Early detection of the disease is critical for slowing its progression and developing appropriate treatment plans. In recent years, artificial intelligence and deep learning methods have begun to play a significant role in clinical decision support systems, particularly due to their high accuracy rates in the analysis of Magnetic Resonance (MR) images. Methods: In this study, a hybrid model was developed for the automatic classification of MS. Two different architectures were used for feature extraction in the developed model. These architectures were selected from among the most successful architectures out of 10 different Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) and Vision Transformer (ViT) architectures. Six different classifiers were used to classify the feature maps obtained in the proposed model and pre-trained models. The application of the VOTE operation in the final stage of the proposed model improved its performance. Results: The proposed model yielded competitive results compared to similar studies in the literature and the CNN and ViT architectures used in this study. The accuracy rate achieved with the proposed hybrid model was 97.28%. Conclusions: These results indicate that the proposed model has the potential to support computer-aided MS detection and may provide a useful framework for clinical decision support systems.

results.title: TurboRhythmPat and Directed Rhythm Lobish: An Explainable Multi-Selector EEG Model for Recognising Attack and Post-Attack States in Multiple Sclerosis.
results.summary: Background/Objectives: Multiple sclerosis (MS) advances through attacks and partial recoveries, yet electroencephalography (EEG) has hardly been used to recognise an attack from the period that follows it, and most EEG models neither test unseen patients nor show which rhythm and electrode pair shaped a decision. Methods: We present an explainable model built around TurboRhythmPat, a feature extractor that codes each 15 s, 19-channel segment as 1805 addressable source-rhythm-target routes in five EEG rhythms. Four iterative feature selectors and their six pairwise intersections form ten selector branches, a self-organised k-nearest-neighbour classifier (tkNN) labels every branch, and iterative majority voting fuses the branch outputs. Directed Rhythm Lobish (DRLobish) decodes the routes behind the selected output into rhythm and electrode-pair statements. We analysed 57 recordings from 19 patients recorded during and after an attack and from 19 healthy controls. Results: Under fully nested leave-one-subject-out validation, in which every data-driven choice was made within the training participants, the attack and post-attack recordings of unseen patients were separated with 65.61% segment-level and 76.32% recording-level accuracy, and patient-level accuracy exceeded chance in 13 of 19 patients (Wilcoxon p = 0.0022). The between-person tasks did not exceed chance (37.92%, 52.51% and 33.17%), and the non-nested estimates (85.71% for attack versus post-attack) were inflated by model selection on the test participants. A permutation-based maxT test over all 1805 routes found no route after family-wise correction (smallest adjusted p = 0.076). Conclusions: Because the attack recording always came first, treatment timing was not documented, no dedicated artefact correction was applied, and the controls were older, the differences are not interpreted as relapse-related changes, and larger prospective cohorts are needed before clinical use.

results.title: Molecularly Aged Protein States as Targets for Drug Design and Delivery in Neurodegenerative Diseases
results.summary: <jats:p>Neurodegenerative drug discovery usually represents a protein target by its gene, canonical sequence, and one or a few structures. That representation can miss the molecular history accumulated by proteins that persist in the brain. Spontaneous chemistry, incomplete repair, altered turnover, proteolysis, phase transitions, and assembly remodeling generate states that may differ from the canonical target in exposure, function, and therapeutic accessibility. We call compositionally resolved species age-generated proteoforms and use molecularly aged protein states when the exact composition remains uncertain. This Review develops a target-state framework for Alzheimer disease, Parkinson disease, amyotrophic lateral sclerosis and frontotemporal dementia, Huntington disease, and multiple sclerosis. It separates detection from age association, causality, brain exposure, proximal target engagement, and clinical evidence. Disease-specific analyses connect tau and amyloid-beta proteoforms, alpha-synuclein and lysosomal or mitochondrial assemblies, TDP-43 loss-of-function states, and persistent myelin or extracellular-matrix states to rational modalities and critical validation experiments. Repair, selective removal, stabilization, state-selective antibodies and small molecules, intrabodies, replacement, and synthesis control are evaluated together with blood–brain barrier transport, cellular and organelle access, pharmacokinetics, and pharmacodynamics. Each class of target state is mapped to the delivery constraint it imposes and the platform for which a precedent exists, and the exposure requirements that state selectivity implies are set out explicitly, including the fraction of a pool that must be engaged, the duration required to move a slowly accumulating state, and the consequences for dosing interval and pharmacodynamic biomarker choice. The aggregate-directed amyloid antibodies are analysed as the existing clinical test of the framework and of its limits. Machine learning remains central to proteoform identification, multimodal prioritization, structure modeling, and molecular design, provided that labels and prospective tests preserve target-state identity. Classical quantum chemistry can address bounded reaction and recognition problems. Quantum computing is treated as an exploratory implementation that requires matched classical baselines and explicit resources. The central requirement is not that an old protein be abnormal, but that a defined disease-relevant state can be selectively engaged while preserving the functional pool.</jats:p>

results.title: Recent Advances in the Multidisciplinary Management of Multiple Sclerosis
results.summary:
<jats:sec>
<jats:title>Abstract:</jats:title>
<jats:p>Multiple Sclerosis (MS) is a chronic neuro-immune demyelinating disease of the central
nervous system that is associated with neurodegeneration and progressive disability. Because of its
diverse clinical presentation and multifactorial etiology, managing MS requires an interdisciplinary
approach that extends beyond traditional pharmacotherapy. This article provides an overview of recent
developments in the multidisciplinary treatment of MS, the pathophysiology of MS, Disease-
Modifying Therapies (DMTs), symptom management strategies, rehabilitation, lifestyle modification,
and the use of new digital health technologies. Adaptive and innate pathways, Blood-Brain Barrier
(BBB) dysfunction, demyelination, and neurodegeneration are considered a critical part of the immune
response that is discussed in terms of clinical manifestations and treatments. The development
of DMTs, including injectable immunomodulators, oral agents, antibodies with monoclonal properties,
and new Bruton’s tyrosine kinase inhibitors are discussed, and their efficacy, safety, and the ability
to select personalized treatment are of key concern. Specific symptom management of motor dysfunction,
pain, fatigue, and cognitive impairment is discussed, and evidence-based rehabilitation approaches
that leverage neuroplasticity to enhance functional outcomes are discussed. The article identifies
multidisciplinary models of care that engage neurologists, rehabilitation specialists, nurses, and
mental health professionals to provide patient-centered care of MS. It highlights lifestyle changes,
complementary therapies, telemedicine, wearables, artificial intelligence, and digital therapeutics as
some of the strategies that can be used to improve disease control, long-term outcomes, and promote
precision, coordinated care.</jats:p>
</jats:sec>

results.title: Management Strategies for Trigeminal Neuralgia: A Systematic Review and Pooled Analysis
results.summary:
<jats:sec>
<jats:title>Purpose:</jats:title>
<jats:p>Trigeminal neuralgia (TN) is one of the most debilitating neuropathic facial pain disorders. Although carbamazepine remains the first-line pharmacologic therapy, many patients become refractory or intolerant to long-term medication, necessitating surgical intervention. Multiple operative techniques are available; however, comparative durability and complication profiles remain heterogeneous. This systematic review aimed to evaluate the effectiveness, recurrence rates, and safety of pharmacologic and surgical management strategies for TN.</jats:p>
</jats:sec>
<jats:sec>
<jats:title>Methods:</jats:title>
<jats:p>A systematic review was conducted in accordance with PRISMA 2020 guidelines. Electronic databases including PubMed, MEDLINE, Embase, and the Cochrane Library were searched for studies evaluating medical and surgical treatments of TN. Randomized controlled trials, prospective and retrospective cohort studies, and systematic reviews reporting measurable pain outcomes were included. Primary outcomes were immediate pain relief and long-term pain freedom (≥3 y). Secondary outcomes included recurrence rates, sensory complications, and quality-of-life measures.</jats:p>
</jats:sec>
<jats:sec>
<jats:title>Results:</jats:title>
<jats:p>Twenty-nine studies met inclusion criteria. Carbamazepine demonstrated effective initial pain control but limited long-term durability due to adverse effects and recurrence. Microvascular decompression (MVD) provided the highest immediate relief (94%) and durable long-term pain freedom (72%). Percutaneous procedures (radiofrequency thermocoagulation, balloon compression, glycerol rhizotomy) showed high initial relief (85%–91%) but increased recurrence and sensory morbidity. Stereotactic radiosurgery demonstrated moderate long-term control with low perioperative morbidity but delayed onset of action. Outcomes in multiple sclerosis-associated TN were inferior compared with classic TN.</jats:p>
</jats:sec>
<jats:sec>
<jats:title>Conclusions:</jats:title>
<jats:p>Microvascular decompression remains the gold standard surgical intervention for medically refractory classic TN in appropriate candidates. Percutaneous and radiosurgical techniques offer effective alternatives for elderly or medically compromised patients. Standardized outcome reporting and high-quality comparative trials are required to refine treatment algorithms.</jats:p>
</jats:sec>
